prerequisites: Having passed Physics I and II, Mathematics I and II from the first year, and Advanced Mathematics and Thermal Engineering from the first semester of the second year.

learning_outcomes.text: Students should be able to gather and interpret relevant data (usually within their field of study) to make judgments that include reflection on relevant social, scientific, or ethical issues.

Students should know how to apply their knowledge to their work or vocation in a professional way and possess the competencies typically demonstrated through the development and defense of arguments and problem-solving within their field of study.
Students should be able to transmit information, ideas, problems, and solutions to both specialized and non-specialized audiences.
Ability to apply new technologies, including information and communication technologies.
Knowledge of applied thermodynamics and heat transfer. Basic principles and their application to solving engineering problems.
Knowledge of the basic principles of fluid mechanics and their application to solving problems in the field of engineering. Calculation of pipes, channels, and fluid systems.

syllabus_topics: Introduction to the study of Fluid Mechanics.
What is a fluid? Properties.
Viscosity and Newton's law. Non-Newtonian fluids.
What does the technician need to know about fluids? Objectives and fundamental simplifications.
Basic concepts. Strategy in the study of fluids.
Fluidostatics.
Forces on fluids: volumetric and superficial. Stress tensor.
Pressure and pressure field. Fundamental equation of hydrostatics. Implications.
Archimedes' principle. Forces on surfaces. Examples.
Kinematics of fluids. Fluid field.
Trajectory, path, and streamline. Steady flow. Uniform flow.
Conservation laws in integral form. Introduction.
Conservation laws. Reynolds transport theorem. Continuity equation.
Energy equation. Linear and angular momentum equation.
Physical interpretation of equations. Applications.
Dimensional analysis and physical similarity.
Foundation of dimensional analysis. Buckingham's theorem. Calculation of dimensionless quantities. Physical interpretation. Similarity.
Flow in conduits. Introduction.
Energy losses in internal and external flows.
Head losses in pipes: empirical equations.
Head losses in pipes: Darcy-Weissbach equation. Friction factor.
Dependence of the friction factor on roughness. Dependence of the friction factor on the Reynolds number: laminar solution and the turbulent problem.
Equations for calculating the friction factor. Colebrook equation. Natural and artificial roughness.
Methods for calculating the friction factor in turbulent flow: iterations, approximate formulas, and diagrams. Moody diagram.
Local losses. Methods for calculating local losses.
Introduction to open channel flow. Introduction and basic concepts.
Dimensional Analysis of the general problem.
Classification of open channel flows.
Uniform flow: losses; analysis and design of installations; optimal section.
Varied flow: specific energy; critical depth; frictionless flow in rectangular channels; hydraulic jumps.
Gradually varied flow: general equation formulation and basic solutions.
Meters and weirs.
Fluidostatics practical session (P1).
Conservation equations practical session (P2).
Introduction to CFD or aerodynamics practical session (P3).
Ideal flow and meters practical session (P4).
Head losses practical session (P5).
teaching_methods: Explanation of theory and general examples

assessment_methods.method: Attendance and/or participation in in-person and/or virtual activities
Theoretical and practical concepts of the subject (written test)
Completion of assignments, cases or exercises

assessment_rules: A minimum grade in the final exam and in the practicals is required to calculate the final average. The completion of practicals is mandatory. If a student has not attended all laboratory practical sessions, they will not be able to take the exam for the subject and, therefore, will not be graded.
